author: anisha
title: You don’t need an iPhone: shoot your first video on the phone you already have
dek: Most first videos fail on light, sound and nerves, not on the camera. Here’s how to get a clean, watchable first video out of a ₹12,000 Android phone, plus the three cheap things worth buying later.
takeaways: Any phone from the last few years records 1080p video that is good enough for YouTube.
Use the back camera, lock focus and exposure, and face a window.
Sound matters more than picture: get the phone or a mic close to your mouth.
Spend money in this order: a ₹300–700 tripod, then a mic, then light. A new phone comes last.

quiz.q: Which camera on your phone usually records the best video?
quiz.why: The main back camera almost always has the bigger sensor and better lens. Flip the phone, frame once using the front camera, then switch.

quiz.q: What should you fix first if viewers leave in the first minute?
o: Your sound and your opening lines
quiz.why: People forgive soft video. They leave quickly when they can’t hear you clearly or the start drags.

quiz.q: Where should the window be when you film yourself indoors?
o: In front of you or to one side
quiz.why: Facing a window lights your face. A window behind you turns you into a silhouette.

author: neeraj
title: The recipe for a good video: hook, promise, payoff
dek: Good YouTube videos look different on the surface and follow the same recipe underneath. Here’s the three-part structure we use for every script, with a worked example you can copy.
takeaways: Open with the hook: the problem or result, in the first few seconds, before any intro.
Say the promise out loud: what the viewer will be able to do by the end.
Deliver the payoff fully, then point to one next video instead of saying goodbye.
Write the one-sentence promise before you write anything else.

quiz.q: What should the first 10 seconds of a tutorial do?
o: Show your channel intro and logo
State the problem or the result the viewer will get
quiz.why: Viewers decide fast. Lead with why they should stay; intros and subscribe requests can wait.

quiz.q: In this recipe, what is the “promise”?
o: What the viewer will be able to do by the end
quiz.why: The promise tells the viewer what they’ll walk away with. The rest of the video has to deliver it.

quiz.q: What’s a better ending than “bye guys, see you next time”?
o: A long recap of every point
Pointing to one specific next video
quiz.why: An end that hands viewers one next video keeps them watching your channel instead of leaving YouTube.

author: neeraj
title: The rules to follow on YouTube: guidelines, copyright, AI and paid promotions
dek: Most channels that get into trouble didn’t mean to break anything. Here are the rules that catch new creators in India most often, explained in plain language, and what to do instead.
takeaways: Community Guidelines strikes expire after 90 days; three active strikes end a channel.
A Content ID claim and a copyright strike are different things. Use music you have the rights to.
Reused or mass-produced content can’t earn money, even if it’s allowed to stay up.
Disclose realistic AI-made content and paid promotions, both on YouTube and under Indian advertising rules.

quiz.q: How many active Community Guidelines strikes lead to a channel being terminated?
quiz.why: YouTube usually starts with a warning; strikes then expire after 90 days, and three active strikes at once terminate the channel.

quiz.q: You used a popular film song in the background. What’s most likely to happen?
o: A Content ID claim, so the rights owner can earn from or block the video
YouTube pays you extra for using a hit
quiz.why: Short clips aren’t automatically allowed. Content ID matches the song and the owner decides what happens. Use YouTube’s Audio Library or licensed music instead.

quiz.q: When does YouTube ask you to disclose AI use?
o: Whenever you used any AI tool at all
When realistic content was generated or meaningfully altered with AI
quiz.why: Disclosure is for realistic content that viewers could mistake for real people, places or events. AI help with scripts or obvious animation doesn’t need it.

author: anisha
title: Light and sound on a budget: what to fix before you buy a camera
short: Light and sound on a budget
dek: A ₹40,000 camera can’t rescue a dark face and an echoing room. A bedsheet, a window and switching off the ceiling fan often can. Here’s our budget playbook for both.
takeaways: Big, soft light flatters faces: a window or a white wall bouncing light beats a bare bulb.
Don’t mix daylight with yellow or white tube light on your face.
Echo comes from hard surfaces. Cloth, curtains and cupboards full of clothes soak it up.
Switch off fans and coolers, record 10 seconds of silence, and always check with headphones.

quiz.q: What makes light look soft and flattering on a face?
o: A small, bright bulb close by
A large light source, like a window or a bounced wall
quiz.why: The bigger the light source compared with your face, the softer the shadows. Windows and white walls are big, free light sources.

quiz.q: Your voice sounds hollow and echoey. What helps most, for free?
o: Moving to a room with curtains, a bed or soft furniture
Turning up the bass in editing
quiz.why: Hard, bare surfaces bounce sound around. Soft furnishings absorb it.

quiz.q: Why record 10 seconds of silence in your room before you start?
o: It gives your editor a clean sample of the room’s background noise
quiz.why: That “room tone” lets noise-reduction tools learn what to remove, and fills gaps between cuts so they don’t sound dead.

author: anisha
title: How to shoot educational videos people actually finish
dek: Teaching on camera is a different skill from teaching in a room. The four formats that work for explainers, how to choose one, and the small production habits that keep learners watching to the end.
takeaways: Teach one idea per video and say what the viewer will be able to do by the end.
Match the format to the subject: talking head, screen recording, hands-on or whiteboard.
Show every example on screen; don’t just describe it.
Add chapters: a 00:00 timestamp plus at least two more in the description.

quiz.q: What’s the best format for teaching how to use a piece of software?
o: A talking head with no visuals
A screen recording with your voice, plus your face briefly
quiz.why: Learners need to see the clicks. Free tools like OBS Studio, or your phone’s built-in screen recorder, are enough.

quiz.q: What do YouTube chapters need to work?
o: Timestamps in the description starting at 00:00, with at least three chapters
quiz.why: Add timestamps in the description starting at 00:00, with at least three chapters, each at least 10 seconds long.

quiz.q: An educational video covers five big topics. What usually works better?
o: One long video covering all five quickly
One video per idea, linked together as a series or playlist
Removing the examples to save time
quiz.why: One idea per video is easier to finish, easier to title, and easier for search to match to the right question.

author: neeraj
title: Your first edit: free editors that work in India, and cuts that keep people watching
dek: CapCut has been blocked in India since 2020, so here’s what to use instead on phones and computers, plus the five edits that matter more than any effect.
takeaways: CapCut is banned in India. VN, DaVinci Resolve, Clipchamp and iMovie are good free options.
Cut silences, false starts and slow intros: that’s most of what “editing” means.
Add captions and on-screen text; many people watch with the sound off.
Keep music well below your voice, and export at the resolution you shot in.

quiz.q: Which free editor is a full professional desktop editor?
quiz.why: DaVinci Resolve’s free version handles editing, colour and audio. It needs a reasonably powerful computer.

quiz.q: What’s usually the most important edit in a beginner’s video?
o: Cutting pauses, mistakes and the slow start
quiz.why: Tight pacing keeps viewers. Effects don’t fix a slow video; cuts do.

quiz.q: Why add captions or on-screen text?
o: Many people watch without sound, and captions help non-native listeners
quiz.why: Muted viewing is common, especially on Shorts and in public places. Text keeps those viewers with you.

author: anisha
title: Titles and thumbnails that earn the click without lying
dek: Your title and thumbnail decide whether anyone presses play. How to make them specific, readable on a phone and honest, plus how to test them without guessing.
takeaways: Plan the title and thumbnail before you film; they’re the promise.
Put the most important words at the start of the title; phones cut long titles.
Thumbnails need one clear subject, few words and strong contrast at a tiny size.
Never promise what the video doesn’t deliver; it costs you viewers and can break policy.

quiz.q: What size should a YouTube thumbnail be?
quiz.why: YouTube recommends 1280 × 720, a 16:9 shape, under 2 MB, as a JPG, PNG or GIF.

quiz.q: Where should the key words in a title go?
o: At the start, because long titles get cut off on phones
quiz.why: Mobile screens truncate long titles. Lead with what the video is about.

quiz.q: What’s the problem with a clickbait thumbnail that the video doesn’t deliver?
o: Viewers leave early, which hurts the video, and misleading thumbnails can be removed
quiz.why: Early exits tell YouTube the video disappointed people, and deceptive thumbnails can break the spam rules.

author: neeraj
title: Shorts and long videos: how to make them help each other
dek: Shorts bring new people; long videos keep them. How the two formats differ, how to connect them, and a simple weekly mix for a small channel.
takeaways: Shorts are vertical and can be up to 3 minutes; they’re for discovery.
Long videos build watch hours, trust and most of a channel’s income.
Shorts watch time doesn’t count towards the long-form watch-hours goal for monetisation.
Link each Short to a related long video, and remake ideas for the format instead of chopping clips.

quiz.q: How long can a YouTube Short be?
quiz.why: Since October 2024, vertical or square videos up to 3 minutes can be uploaded as Shorts.

quiz.q: Does watch time from the Shorts feed count towards the long-form watch-hours requirement for the Partner Programme?
quiz.why: Shorts have their own route (Shorts views in 90 days). Long-form watch hours come from public long videos.

quiz.q: What’s a good way to turn a long video into Shorts?
o: Pick one strong moment and reframe it vertically with its own hook
quiz.why: Shorts need their own hook in the first second and a vertical frame. A random chunk usually starts mid-thought.

author: neeraj
title: How YouTube creators get paid, and what changes on 1 February 2027
dek: The YouTube Partner Programme’s entry bar for ad earnings doubles for new applicants on 1 February 2027. Here’s what the requirements are, what’s changing, and the income that doesn’t depend on them.
takeaways: Fan funding (memberships, Super Thanks and more) starts at 500 subscribers.
Ad revenue needs 1,000 subscribers plus 4,000 watch hours or 10 million Shorts views, until 31 January 2027.
From 1 February 2027, new applicants need 8,000 watch hours or 20 million Shorts views; channels already in are not affected.
Brand deals, affiliates and your own products often pay more than ads for small channels.

quiz.q: From 1 February 2027, how many qualified watch hours will new channels need for ad revenue?
quiz.why: YouTube announced in August 2026 that new applicants will need 8,000 qualified watch hours in 12 months, or 20 million qualified Shorts views in 90 days. The 1,000-subscriber requirement stays.

quiz.q: Which of these counts as a qualified watch hour?
o: Watch time on an unlisted video
Watch time on a public long video
Views from your own ad campaign
Watch time on a deleted video
quiz.why: Only public long-form videos (and archived live streams) count. Private, unlisted and deleted videos, ad views and Shorts watch time don’t.

quiz.q: Do channels already in the Partner Programme have to meet the new 2027 thresholds?
o: No, the new entry bar applies to new applicants
quiz.why: Existing members aren’t affected by the new entry requirements, though everyone has to keep following the monetisation policies.

author: anisha
title: Reading YouTube Analytics: five numbers and a 30-minute weekly routine
short: Five numbers and a weekly routine
dek: YouTube Studio shows you dozens of charts. Five of them answer almost every question a small channel has. Here they are, what “good” looks like, and the weekly routine that turns them into decisions.
takeaways: Impressions click-through rate tells you whether the title and thumbnail work.
Average view duration and the retention graph tell you whether the video works.
Traffic sources tell you how people found you; returning viewers tell you whether they came back.
Compare each video with your own recent videos, not with other channels, and change one thing at a time.

quiz.q: Which number tells you whether your title and thumbnail are working?
quiz.why: Click-through rate is the share of people who saw your thumbnail and clicked. It’s mostly about packaging.

quiz.q: Your retention graph drops sharply in the first 30 seconds. What should you look at?
o: Your opening: the hook and how fast you get to the point
quiz.why: An early drop means the start didn’t match what people expected, or took too long to get going.

quiz.q: What’s the fairest comparison for a new video’s numbers?
o: Your own recent videos at the same age
quiz.why: Channels differ hugely. Compare with your own videos after the same number of days.

author: anisha
title: Write the one sentence your brand stands on
dek: Before colours, before a logo, before the mood board you’re itching to make: one sentence that says who you’re for and why you’re different. If a competitor could sign it, it isn’t finished.
takeaways: Write your positioning as one sentence: who it’s for, what they need, what you are, how you’re different, and why anyone should believe it.
Test it: if a competitor could put their name on it, it’s too vague. Rewrite until they couldn’t.
Do this before any design work. Every visual decision later is easier when the sentence exists.

quiz.q: What makes a positioning sentence useful?
quiz.why: If a competitor could put their name on it, it doesn’t describe what makes you different.

quiz.q: Which part of the sentence is the proof?
o: The reason to believe the difference
quiz.why: The proof is the checkable reason someone should believe your claim: a process, a person, a number.

quiz.q: When should you write the brand sentence?
quiz.why: Every design and copy decision is easier and more consistent when the sentence already exists.

author: anisha
title: A logo that survives at 16 pixels
dek: Your logo will spend most of its life tiny: a browser tab, an app icon, a profile picture in someone’s notifications. Design for that first and the big version takes care of itself.
takeaways: Test every logo idea at 16, 32 and 64 pixels before you fall in love with it. Browser tabs and profile pictures are where people actually see it.
Plan a set, not one file: a full lockup, a short version or symbol, and a one-colour version.
Deliver SVG for the web and print, plus PNGs for social profiles, so nobody has to screenshot your logo.

quiz.q: Why test a logo at 16 pixels?
o: Browsers show tab icons about that small
quiz.why: Favicons in browser tabs and bookmarks are around 16 to 32 pixels, and that’s where many people first see a logo.

quiz.q: Which file format scales without losing quality?
quiz.why: SVG is a vector format, so it stays sharp at any size.

quiz.q: Which version should every logo have besides full colour?
quiz.why: A one-colour version works on photos, in print and anywhere colour isn’t available.

author: anisha
title: Colour and type: build a system, not a mood board
dek: A palette isn’t a list of colours you like. It’s a set of jobs: which colour means action, which one is background, which one you almost never use. Same for type. Write it down and everyone, human or AI, gets it right.
takeaways: Keep the palette small: one main colour, one or two accents, and neutrals. Give each colour a job.
Check contrast: body text should be at least 4.5:1 against its background to meet WCAG AA.
Two type families are plenty for most brands, with a simple size scale.
Write exact values (hex, RGB, font names, sizes) so designers, developers and AI tools all use the same thing.

quiz.q: What contrast ratio does WCAG AA ask for with normal body text?
quiz.why: WCAG 2 level AA asks for at least 4.5 to 1 for normal-size text.

quiz.q: How many type families does a small brand usually need?
quiz.why: A display face plus a readable text face, or one versatile family, covers almost everything.

quiz.q: Why give each colour a job?
o: So people and tools use it consistently
quiz.why: Rules like “orange is only for buttons” are easy for designers, developers and AI tools to follow.

author: neeraj
title: How Meta decides who sees your ad, and why creative is now your targeting
dek: You used to win on Meta by picking clever interests. Now the system mostly finds people for you, and the strongest signal it has is your ad itself. Here’s how the auction works, in plain English, and what it means for a small budget.
takeaways: Meta runs an auction for every ad slot. The winner isn’t simply the highest bid: it’s the best mix of bid, estimated action rate and ad quality.
With broad targeting, your creative does most of the targeting, because the people who respond to an ad teach the system who to show it to.
An ad set needs roughly 50 optimisation events within 7 days to leave the learning phase, so small budgets should use fewer ad sets, not more.
Different creative concepts reach different people. Five versions of one idea are mostly one ad.

quiz.q: Which three things decide who wins Meta’s ad auction?
o: Bid, estimated action rate and ad quality
quiz.why: Meta combines your bid, how likely the person is to act, and the ad’s quality into a total value.

quiz.q: Roughly how many optimisation events does an ad set need to leave the learning phase?
quiz.why: Meta’s guidance is around 50 optimisation events within a 7-day period.

quiz.q: With broad targeting, what does most of the targeting work?
o: Your creative and who responds to it
How long the ad text is
quiz.why: People who respond to an ad teach the system who else to show it to, so different ideas reach different people.

author: neeraj
title: The five numbers that matter, and the vanity ones to ignore
dek: Ads Manager shows you about two hundred columns. Five of them tell you almost everything, and they also tell you which part of your funnel is broken. Here they are, with one formula that ties them together.
takeaways: Watch CPM, link CTR, cost per click, conversion rate and cost per result (or ROAS). Together they show where a campaign breaks.
Cost per result is roughly CPM divided by 1,000, times CTR, times conversion rate, flipped. Improve any one and the result gets cheaper.
High CPM points at audience or ad quality, low CTR at the hook, good CTR with few sales at the landing page or offer.
Likes and reach alone are vanity metrics for a sales campaign.

quiz.q: Good CTR but almost no purchases usually points to…
quiz.why: If people click but don’t buy, the ad did its job; the page, price or offer didn’t.

quiz.q: CPM means…
quiz.why: CPM is cost per mille: what you pay for 1,000 impressions.

quiz.q: Which is a vanity metric for a sales campaign?
quiz.why: Likes don’t pay. For a sales campaign, judge cost per purchase and return on ad spend.

author: neeraj
title: A 30-minute weekly routine for small ad accounts
dek: Small ad accounts die two ways: neglect, or being fiddled with every morning. Here’s the routine we use instead: once a week, half an hour, a few clear rules and a log.
takeaways: Check once a week, not every morning. Significant edits can restart the learning phase and make results harder to read.
Use a simple kill rule: if an ad has spent about two to three times your target cost per result with nothing to show, pause it.
Refresh creative when frequency rises and CTR falls, typically every few weeks for a small audience.
Change one thing at a time and write it down, so you know what actually worked.

quiz.q: Why avoid editing ad sets every day?
o: Significant edits can restart the learning phase
quiz.why: Big changes can send an ad set back into learning, making results noisy and harder to read.

quiz.q: Which is a sign your creative is getting tired?
quiz.why: When the same people see an ad more often and click less, it’s time for new creative.

quiz.q: How many things should one test change?
quiz.why: Change one thing at a time so you know what caused the result.

author: neeraj
title: How AI search picks what to quote
dek: When someone asks ChatGPT, Perplexity or Google’s AI for the best design studio or the cheapest way to run Meta ads, the answer is built from web pages. Here’s roughly how those pages get picked, and the first things to check on your own site.
takeaways: AI search tools look things up on the web, pick a handful of pages, then summarise them. If they can’t find or crawl your page, you can’t be quoted.
Make sure AI crawlers aren’t blocked in robots.txt, for example OAI-SearchBot for ChatGPT search and PerplexityBot for Perplexity.
ChatGPT search draws on third-party search providers, so being well indexed in Bing as well as Google helps.
Pages that answer a question clearly, near the top, from a source that looks trustworthy are the easiest to quote.

quiz.q: Before an AI search tool can quote your page, it must be able to…
quiz.why: If a page can’t be found and read, it can’t be used in an answer.

quiz.q: Which robots.txt user agent belongs to OpenAI’s search crawler?
quiz.why: OAI-SearchBot is the crawler OpenAI uses for ChatGPT search results.

quiz.q: What kind of page is easiest for an AI tool to quote?
o: One that answers the question clearly near the top
A page that is only images
quiz.why: Clear, early answers in plain text are easy to find, read and cite.

author: neeraj
title: Write answer-first pages
dek: The old blog habit was a long story first and the answer somewhere near paragraph nine. Readers hated it, and AI tools skip it. Put the answer at the top, then earn the scroll.
takeaways: Answer the main question in the first one or two sentences, then add the detail.
Use headings phrased the way people ask, like “How much does a logo cost?”, so readers and AI tools find the right section.
Use tables for comparisons, lists for steps and short paragraphs for everything else.
End with a short FAQ that answers the next questions people ask, in plain sentences.

quiz.q: Where should the direct answer go?
quiz.why: Put the answer in the first one or two sentences, then add detail.

quiz.q: Why use question-style headings?
o: They match how people ask search and AI tools
quiz.why: Headings phrased as real questions help skimmers and give AI tools clear question-and-answer pairs.

quiz.q: Which format is best for a comparison?
quiz.why: Tables are easy for both people and machines to read and compare.

author: neeraj
title: Proof, structure and freshness: why AI trusts some pages
dek: Two pages say the same thing. One gets quoted, one gets ignored. Usually the difference is proof (who says so and how they know), structure (can a machine tell what’s what) and freshness (is this still true).
takeaways: Show your proof: named authors with real expertise, sources linked for every claim, and first-hand evidence like tests and your own numbers.
Add structure machines understand: clear headings, dates, and schema markup such as Article, FAQPage and Organization.
Keep important pages fresh and say when they were last checked. Outdated facts get dropped.
Measure it: ask AI tools your category questions each month and note who they cite, and watch branded search.

quiz.q: What is llms.txt?
o: A proposed file that gives AI tools a map of your site
quiz.why: It’s a proposed convention for a plain-text site map for AI tools. Cheap to add, but not a guaranteed ranking factor.

quiz.q: Which of these is first-hand evidence?
o: A test you ran with your own numbers
quiz.why: Original tests and measurements are evidence nobody else can copy.

quiz.q: How can you check whether AI tools mention your brand?
o: Ask them your customers’ questions regularly and note who they cite
quiz.why: There’s no perfect report yet, so a monthly manual check is the most reliable method.
